frameworks.name: Automated Service Business (Call-Capture Arbitrage)
frameworks.definition: A three-role system: Google Business profiles generate inbound calls, a Philippines-based VA answers and books appointments, and a local contractor fulfills the job; operator collects the spread.

claims.text: In a local-service arbitrage model where Google Business profiles generate inbound calls (e.g., car detailing), the operator charges the customer roughly $250, pays the fulfillment contractor $100-$150, and retains approximately $100 per job in profit. At two to three jobs per day this yields $200-$300 in daily profit, or roughly $6,000-$9,000 per month before scaling.
claims.speaker: unnamed young entrepreneur (15k_10_mins_work_virtual_assistants.txt)
conditions: Local service category (car detailing cited as primary example)
Inbound calls sourced exclusively via Google Business profile
Fulfillment subcontracted to local operator, not employed staff
claims.mechanism: Operator controls the customer relationship and brand; contractor provides only labor at below-retail cost, creating a spread the operator captures without performing any fulfillment.

numbers.axis: per-job economics in local service arbitrage (car detailing)

bounded_by: Speaker does not claim this margin holds for industries with higher contractor market rates
Model requires category where Google Business profile generates sufficient call volume organically

claims.text: A single Google Business profile for a local service (e.g., car detailing) with photos, reviews, and an accurate address generates roughly one to two inbound appointment requests per day within six months of setup. The speaker's profile generated 511 customer interactions in the last six months at time of recording.

claims.text: Philippines-based virtual assistants capable of answering phones, booking appointments, and doing basic administrative work (Google Sheets, customer communication) are available at $3-$5 per hour, with speaker's experience placing highest-quality VAs at $4-$5 per hour. Equivalent US-based staff for the same role would cost roughly $15-$25 per hour, making Philippines sourcing a 3-5x labor cost advantage.

claims.text: Requiring VA job applicants to submit a voice recording as part of their application effectively filters out candidates with accents too strong for comfortable customer phone interactions. Speaker treats absence of a voice recording as an automatic disqualifier.

Job platform allows open-text job description (e.g., onlinejobs.ph)
claims.mechanism: Voice recording submission creates an asynchronous accent pre-screen without requiring the operator to conduct initial calls with every applicant; it shifts the screening burden to the candidate and surfaces the single make-or-break qualification (spoken English fluency) before any operator time is invested.
bounded_by: Speaker acknowledges slight accents are acceptable ('as long as they're mostly pretty good at speaking English'); the filter is for comprehensibility, not accent elimination

claims.text: In the local service arbitrage model described, hiring a VA is only economically justified once the business is already generating two to three jobs per day, because at that volume the VA's salary ($1,000-$1,500/month) is covered by a fraction of the daily profit ($200-$300/day) and the hire becomes cash-flow positive immediately.

Operator currently answering calls personally (i.e., the VA replaces operator time)
claims.mechanism: The VA's cost is fully funded by the existing profit stream at 2-3 jobs/day, so the hire does not introduce financial risk; it frees founder time without reducing net profit.

claims.text: When sourcing a local fulfillment contractor for a service arbitrage business, targeting small owner-operated businesses (identified by low-budget websites and low price lists) rather than established branded companies produces contractors who will accept below-market per-job rates in exchange for guaranteed booking volume.

claims.mechanism: Small operators face unpredictable demand and are willing to discount per-job rate in exchange for predictable guaranteed volume; the guaranteed flow is worth more to them than the margin difference, while the operator keeps the spread.

examples.text: In a recorded call played in the video, a Philippines-based VA answered an inbound inquiry for the speaker's mobile car detailing business. The VA described the interior and exterior detail service, quoted $250 for both, confirmed mobile service availability, asked for water and electricity access, offered a 3-4pm appointment slot for the same day, and collected the customer's full address — all without operator involvement. The customer booked a 4pm appointment. The call illustrated that a well-scripted VA can handle pricing, scheduling, upsell (mobile service framing), and logistics end-to-end.

The speaker showed a scheduling sheet from roughly one year prior to recording. On the busiest days shown, the sheet recorded 8, 9, 10, and 15 appointment slots including cancellations in a single day, all handled by a VA. This demonstrated that a single VA, given a clear script and booking sheet, can manage high daily appointment volume that would be unmanageable for a solo operator answering calls personally.

The speaker searched 'car detailing Manitoba' and pulled up a small operator, Gooner Auto Care, to demonstrate the contractor sourcing method. The site listed interior detailing at $70-$75 and a premium package at ~$190. The speaker used this as a live example of a viable volume-deal candidate: a small owner-run business with public pricing well below the $250 the operator charges customers, leaving a negotiable margin of roughly $75-$150 per job if the contractor accepts a volume deal.

The speaker played a voice recording from an older VA applicant to demonstrate the accent evaluation process. The applicant's English was described as 'slightly' accented but comprehensible — speaker's verdict was 'fine' and 'good to go.' The example set an explicit calibration point: a slight non-native accent is acceptable as long as the applicant can be understood; a heavy foreign-sounding accent would disqualify the candidate.

practices.text: Post the VA job on onlinejobs.ph, not free platforms; use the paid tier and specify full-time employment, $1,000-$1,500/month salary, communication/customer service/Google Sheets as required skills, and make a neutral English accent plus a voice or video recording submission non-negotiable in the job description.

Give the VA a written script for answering calls, a Google Sheet template to log each appointment (time, day, job price, contractor cost, profit, contractor contact, notes), and clear instructions before they start; do not rely on verbal briefing alone.

Create a Google Business profile for the service category (e.g., car detailing) in each target area, add photos and gather reviews, then let the profile generate organic inbound calls; no paid ads required in early stage.

When prospecting local contractors for fulfillment partnerships, look for small owner-operated businesses with low-budget websites and low public pricing; avoid large branded operations. Pitch the volume guarantee ('2-3 bookings a day') as the negotiating lever to secure below-public-rate per-job pricing.

Do not hire a VA until you are already receiving enough inbound calls to confirm the VA's monthly salary will be covered by the existing profit stream; use VA as a scale enabler, not an early-stage experiment.
